power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: We also thank the professionals from the second-chance school who provided qualitative feedback on the comprehensibility and cross-cultural recognizability of the visual stimuli during instrument development.
Ultra-short assessment formats reduce respondent burden, fatigue, and administration time, but psychometric compression is not only an administrative operation.

Shortening a measure reduces the number of observations available for content sampling, reliability, and construct representation, and it can weaken the evidence for the intended score interpretation when item reduction is guided mainly by convenience rather than by theory and validation evidence (American Educational Research Association et al., 2014; Messick, 1995; Smith et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Shortening a measure reduces the number of observations available for content sampling, reliability, and construct representation, and it can weaken the evidence for the intended score interpretation when item reduction is guided mainly by convenience rather than by theory and validation evidence <ref type="bibr">(American Educational Research Association et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Messick, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Smith et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: This concern becomes sharper when compression is combined with nontraditional response formats or stimuli, because the information lost may concern not only content breadth but also the response process that links stimuli to the intended construct (Messick, 1995; Wetzel & Greiff, 2018).
text.formatted: This concern becomes sharper when compression is combined with nontraditional response formats or stimuli, because the information lost may concern not only content breadth but also the response process that links stimuli to the intended construct <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Messick, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Wetzel & Greiff, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Paired-comparison methods provide one possible response-format alternative.

Their psychometric roots lie in Thurstone's comparative judgment model and subsequent pairedcomparison scaling and structural-equation work, and they have also been used in applied preference and decision contexts where graded strength of preference is informative (Bech et al., 2007; Bramley, 2007; Maydeu-Olivares & Böckenholt, 2005; Thurstone, 1927).
text.formatted: Their psychometric roots lie in Thurstone's comparative judgment model and subsequent pairedcomparison scaling and structural-equation work, and they have also been used in applied preference and decision contexts where graded strength of preference is informative <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bech et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bramley, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Maydeu-Olivares & Böckenholt, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Thurstone, 1927)</ref>.

text.text: Modern forcedchoice and paired-comparison models can recover normative trait information under appropriate design conditions, but the format does not guarantee validity by itself; the pair structure, scoring model, and construct representation remain central (Brown, 2016; Brown & Maydeu-Olivares, 2011; Maydeu-Olivares & Brown, 2010).
text.formatted: Modern forcedchoice and paired-comparison models can recover normative trait information under appropriate design conditions, but the format does not guarantee validity by itself; the pair structure, scoring model, and construct representation remain central <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Brown, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Brown & Maydeu-Olivares, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Maydeu-Olivares & Brown, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The present article focuses on graded paired comparisons (GPCs), not strictly binary forced choice.
In a GPC item, respondents indicate both the direction and the strength of their preference or self-description.

This distinction matters because dichotomizing a comparative response discards preference-strength information, whereas graded responses preserve orderedcategory information that may improve score recovery if the response categories are interpretable (Bech et al., 2007; Brown & Maydeu-Olivares, 2018; Stark et al., 2005).
text.formatted: This distinction matters because dichotomizing a comparative response discards preference-strength information, whereas graded responses preserve orderedcategory information that may improve score recovery if the response categories are interpretable <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bech et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Brown & Maydeu-Olivares, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Stark et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, graded responses may introduce their own threshold and response-style complications, so the format should be evaluated as a measurement design rather than as a generic improvement over ratings or binary choices (Brown & Maydeu-Olivares, 2018; Wetzel & Carstensen, 2017; Wetzel et al., 2020).
text.formatted: At the same time, graded responses may introduce their own threshold and response-style complications, so the format should be evaluated as a measurement design rather than as a generic improvement over ratings or binary choices <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Brown & Maydeu-Olivares, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Wetzel & Carstensen, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Wetzel et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Image-based GPC assessment adds a further layer of design risk.
Images can be fast, engaging, and semantically rich, and image-based comparative assessment has shown empirical promise in personality assessment (Hilliard et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Images can be fast, engaging, and semantically rich, and image-based comparative assessment has shown empirical promise in personality assessment <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Hilliard et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, images are high-dimensional stimuli: a photograph can carry target-trait content alongside visual salience, affective tone, familiarity, social desirability, cultural associations, and idiosyncratic preferences.

From a validity perspective, the key question is therefore not whether images are appealing, but whether the image-pair response process preserves construct-relevant information and limits constructirrelevant variance (American Educational Research Association et al., 2014; Hilliard et al., 2022; Messick, 1995).
text.formatted: From a validity perspective, the key question is therefore not whether images are appealing, but whether the image-pair response process preserves construct-relevant information and limits constructirrelevant variance <ref type="bibr">(American Educational Research Association et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Hilliard et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Messick, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: A narrower measurement question must be separated from the broader validity question: how much target-relevant information remains in an ultra-short response pattern?
Information recovery refers to the extent to which scores from an ultra-short response pattern recover either a known latent target or an observed benchmark score.

It is narrower than validity, because benchmark recovery cannot establish content representation, response-process validity, fairness, or appropriate use by itself; nevertheless, poor benchmark recovery is a serious warning sign for any intended interpretation (American Educational Research Association et al., 2014; Campbell & Fiske, 1959; Messick, 1995).
text.formatted: It is narrower than validity, because benchmark recovery cannot establish content representation, response-process validity, fairness, or appropriate use by itself; nevertheless, poor benchmark recovery is a serious warning sign for any intended interpretation <ref type="bibr">(American Educational Research Association et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Campbell & Fiske, 1959;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Messick, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: This framing also clarifies the role of supervised prediction.

Cross-validated models can estimate how much benchmark information is recoverable from the response pattern, but they are diagnostic recovery benchmarks rather than psychometric scoring models by themselves (Morris et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Cross-validated models can estimate how much benchmark information is recoverable from the response pattern, but they are diagnostic recovery benchmarks rather than psychometric scoring models by themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Morris et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: We therefore use information recovery as the organizing principle for the present article.
Research on comparative measurement shows that item-pair construction and loading configurations affect forced-choice performance (Sun et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Research on comparative measurement shows that item-pair construction and loading configurations affect forced-choice performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Sun et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: For Thurstonian IRT, previous work has documented statistical limitations (Bürkner et al., 2019) and derived theoretical bounds on information obtainable from ordinal comparative judgments (Bürkner, 2022).
text.formatted: For Thurstonian IRT, previous work has documented statistical limitations <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bürkner et al., 2019)</ref> and derived theoretical bounds on information obtainable from ordinal comparative judgments <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bürkner, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Empirical research has compared graded, dichotomous forced-choice, and Likert formats in terms of psychometric properties and response styles (Zhang et al., 2024), while simulations have examined response categories, ipsativity, and pair composition (Lingel et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Empirical research has compared graded, dichotomous forced-choice, and Likert formats in terms of psychometric properties and response styles <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Zhang et al., 2024)</ref>, while simulations have examined response categories, ipsativity, and pair composition <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Lingel et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Ultrashort pictorial assessment also predates this work: the PPTQ-C uses three paired pictorial contrasts per Big Five dimension (Maćkiewicz & Cieciuch, 2016), although a subsequent evaluation reported limited factorial support (Martins et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Ultrashort pictorial assessment also predates this work: the PPTQ-C uses three paired pictorial contrasts per Big Five dimension <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Maćkiewicz & Cieciuch, 2016)</ref>, although a subsequent evaluation reported limited factorial support <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Martins et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Image-based forced-choice instruments drawing on larger item pools have demonstrated benchmark convergence (Hilliard et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Image-based forced-choice instruments drawing on larger item pools have demonstrated benchmark convergence <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Hilliard et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: What remains less directly characterized is the joint influence of target signal, stimulus properties, pair construction, and systematic nuisance on benchmark recovery from only three graded comparisons.

The present study therefore maps conditional benchmark recovery across these design factors, test length, and response format, including cases in which internal consistency increases while target recovery declines.
The article addresses three questions.
First, which design factors most strongly determine benchmark recovery in ultra-short GPC assessment?
Second, do graded preferences retain more target information than binary paired choices when both are generated from the same latent utilities?
Third, do empirical three-pair image-GPC implementations targeting different construct domains exhibit distinct benchmark-recovery profiles despite sharing the same response format and test length?
Study 1 answers the first two questions through a factorial Monte Carlo simulation.

Study 2 addresses the third question using two brief benchmarks expected to differ in empirical recoverability: the STAI-6 state anxiety short form and the Smartphone Application-Based Addiction Scale (SABAS; Csibi et al., 2018; Marteau & Bekker, 1992; Spielberger, 1983).
text.formatted: Study 2 addresses the third question using two brief benchmarks expected to differ in empirical recoverability: the STAI-6 state anxiety short form and the Smartphone Application-Based Addiction Scale (SABAS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Csibi et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Marteau & Bekker, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Spielberger, 1983)</ref>.

text.text: STAI-6 is a focused state-affective measure designed for brief administration, whereas SABAS is commonly scored as a unidimensional total but covers addiction-component content including salience, mood modification, tolerance, withdrawal, conflict, and relapse (Billieux et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2024; Csibi et al., 2018; Elhai et al., 2017; Mason et al., 2022; Vujić et al., 2024).

text.text: Study 1 evaluated whether ultra-short GPC responses can recover a target trait when construct saturation, stimulus validity, nuisance variance, pair construction, test length, response format, and recovery method are varied.

The simulation followed recommendations for simulation studies as evaluations of statistical and measurement procedures by specifying the datagenerating mechanism, manipulated factors, estimands, performance measures, replication structure, and sensitivity checks (Morris et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The simulation followed recommendations for simulation studies as evaluations of statistical and measurement procedures by specifying the datagenerating mechanism, manipulated factors, estimands, performance measures, replication structure, and sensitivity checks <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Morris et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The main design crossed 324 conditions with 1,000 replications per condition.

Each replication generated N = 375 persons to ensure the Monte Carlo conditions represented the scale of the intended empirical application, generating three response datasets from the same latent utilities: single-stimulus ratings, graded paired comparisons, and binary paired choices.
Holding the latent utilities constant allowed the response formats to be compared without changing the stimulus pool.
The data-generating model included one target trait and one nuisance trait.

Benchmark indicators defined the target to be recovered, which operationalized the idea that an empirical ultra-short task is usually judged against an observed benchmark rather than against a known latent trait (Campbell & Fiske, 1959; Messick, 1995).
text.formatted: Benchmark indicators defined the target to be recovered, which operationalized the idea that an empirical ultra-short task is usually judged against an observed benchmark rather than against a known latent trait <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Campbell & Fiske, 1959;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Messick, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: Stimulus utilities were generated so that target signal could be strong or weak, and so that a systematic nuisance contrast could be absent, moderate, or strong.

Pair construction varied the quality of target contrasts: balanced pairs had clear target direction, asymmetric pairs weakened one side of the target contrast, and contaminated pairs added construct-irrelevant influence.
Test length varied from 3 to 24 pairs.
The three-pair condition was the focal ultra-short design; longer forms indicated when additional comparisons became necessary (Brown & Maydeu-Olivares, 2011; Smith et al., 2000).
text.formatted: The three-pair condition was the focal ultra-short design; longer forms indicated when additional comparisons became necessary <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Brown & Maydeu-Olivares, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Smith et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these factors represented the main design routes by which target information can be preserved, attenuated, or replaced by stable construct-irrelevant responding in an ultra-short comparative task (Brown, 2016; Hilliard et al., 2022; Messick, 1995; Morris et al., 2019; Thurstone, 1927).

Full condition definitions, coding decisions, seeds, Monte Carlo summaries, and output checks are provided in the supplemental materials and reproducible scripts.

Recovery was evaluated with simple and diagnostic scoring indices.
For each response format, we computed oriented sum scores, first principal components, and 10-fold cross-validated ridge prediction of the simulated benchmark.
These indices were not treated as competing operational scoring rules.
They were used to estimate how much target-relevant information was recoverable from the response pattern.
We report correlations with the simulated benchmark, globally calibrated bias, RMSE, alpha, and omega.

To test whether the main conclusions depended on simplifying assumptions in the factorial design, focal robustness simulations decoupled benchmark saturation from stimulus loading and decomposed pair construction into target asymmetry, nuisance contrast, and random judgment noise.
A separate threshold-heterogeneity sensitivity check varied ordinal cut-points across generated indicators and pair responses.
The main result was the design dependence of recovery.
Under balanced pair construction and no nuisance variance, three GPC pairs recovered the benchmark strongly when construct saturation and stimulus validity were high, r = .852.
Recovery remained above the practical r = .70 criterion when construct saturation was high and stimulus validity was moderate, r = .745.
When either construct saturation or stimulus validity was low, three pairs were insufficient and longer forms were needed.
With moderate construct saturation and high stimulus validity, six pairs crossed the criterion; with lower saturation or stimulus validity, even 24 pairs often failed to reach it.

Figure 1 visualizes this interaction: ultra-short recovery appeared in the high-signal region of the design space, whereas weaker construct or stimulus signal required more pairs and often still failed to reach the recovery criterion.

text.text: Nuisance variance created a particularly important warning.
For GPC responses, stronger systematic nuisance variance reduced benchmark recovery but increased internal consistency.
Mean benchmark recovery declined from .582 when nuisance strength was zero to .374 when nuisance strength was .45, whereas omega increased from .695 to .895.
Thus, reliability could reflect stable construct-irrelevant responding.
Pair contamination showed the same pattern: balanced pairs outperformed contaminated pairs in benchmark recovery, despite acceptable reliability under some contaminated conditions.
This dissociation is central because it shows that coherent responding is not necessarily construct-relevant responding.
Average format differences were smaller than the effects of design conditions.
Across all conditions, single-stimulus ratings showed the highest mean benchmark recovery, GPC responses were close behind, and binary paired choices recovered less information.
The average benchmark correlations were .493 for single-stimulus ratings, .477 for GPC responses, and .447 for binary paired choice.
GPC responses also retained more information than binary choices in favorable regions of the design space, supporting the value of graded preference strength over dichotomized choice.
The single-stimulus advantage should be read cautiously because the single-stimulus condition observed two ratings per pair and was an informational reference rather than a burden-equated comparison.
Table 2 summarizes the core contrasts and shows that average format differences were modest relative to changes associated with saturation, validity, nuisance variance, length, and pair construction.

text.text: Metamodels quantified the same pattern.

For benchmark recovery across all response formats, sequential partial eta squared was .812 for construct saturation, .702 for stimulus validity, .661 for pair construction, .648 for nuisance strength, and .445 for test length, compared with .089 for response format.

In GPC condition means, the full metamodel explained 96.1% of the variation in recovery; eta squared was .359 for construct saturation, .203 for stimulus validity, .165 for pair construction, .159 for nuisance strength, and .063 for test length.
Full metamodel tables are reported in the supplemental materials.
The focal simulations supported the same interpretation after decoupling several dependencies in the main design.
Target saturation, stimulus loading, nuisance contrast, judgment noise, pair construction, and length each contributed to recovery.
Stable nuisance contrast was more damaging than random judgment noise in the tested focal design.
The threshold-heterogeneity sensitivity check did not change the qualitative ordering of conclusions across jitter levels.
Taken together, these results locate recovery in the information preserved by a particular benchmark, stimulus set, pair design, response format, and test length.
Study 1 shows why ultra-short GPC assessment should be evaluated as an information-recovery problem.
The response format mattered, but the design conditions mattered more.
Three GPC pairs can recover benchmark information when the target construct is focused, stimuli are strongly aligned with the target, pair construction is balanced, and nuisance variance is low.
The same format can fail when those conditions are absent.
The most consequential warning is that internal consistency can increase for the wrong reason: stable nuisance variance can make responses coherent while pulling them away from the target benchmark.
Simulation results alone cannot establish whether real image-based implementations occupy favorable or unfavorable regions of this design space.
Study 2 therefore examines two three-pair image-GPC implementations using the same response format and scoring framework but different construct domains.
The goal is not to test the causal mechanisms isolated in Study 1, but to assess whether empirical benchmark recovery shows the kind of design dependence predicted by the simulation.
Study 2 applied the simulation framework to an empirical image-based GPC dataset administered online through Qualtrics.
Eligible participants were recruited through universityrelated networks from a general participant pool aged 16 years or older.
A total of 383 participants remained after initial screening, of whom 375 completed all study-measure blocks.
The primary analytic sample comprised 369 participants with complete study-measure and age information.
Six additional participants had complete study-measure responses but did not report their age.
Because the minimum eligibility age was 16 years and age eligibility could not be verified for these cases, they were not included in the primary analytic sample.
Among the 369 participants with complete age data, the mean age was 20.28 years (SD = 5.65; range = 16-64); 239 participants identified as female, 124 as male, and 6 as another gender category.
Participants completed Likert benchmark measures and three-pair image-GPC versions of the same two constructs in a single Qualtrics session.
The design was within-person.
The order of the Likert and GPC blocks was randomized in the survey flow to control for order effects.
No additional exclusion criteria were applied beyond duration, verified-age eligibility, and assessment-block completion criteria.
All participants provided informed consent through the online procedure approved for the eligible age range, including 16-and 17-year-old participants.
The empirical study was approved by the Bioethics Commission of the Universitat de Vic-Universitat Central de Catalunya, internal code 308/2024.

text.text: The observed Likert totals therefore served as empirical benchmarks.
For each construct, the empirical comparative task consisted of three graded image pairs.
Respondents saw two images side by side and answered the prompt, "Which photo best represents your current moment?"
Responses used a five-point bipolar preference scale: strongly prefer left, slightly prefer left, both equally, slightly prefer right, and strongly prefer right.
Thus, the empirical task was a graded paired-comparison preference task, not a strictly binary forcedchoice task (Brown & Maydeu-Olivares, 2018; Stark et al., 2005).

text.text: Candidate images were compiled from open-access image banks, primarily Pexels, using freely licensed real photographs.
Across the two instruments, the initial candidate pool comprised 42 images for STAI and 41 for SABAS, reduced to six final images per measure.
Four expert judges reviewed candidate images for semantic equivalence with the corresponding verbal item, clarity, naturalness, and absence of confusing visual elements.
The procedure used iterative expert consensus inspired by Delphi-style item-development methods (Diamond et al., 2014; Hasson et al., 2000).

text.text: Earlier qualitative response-process feedback from preliminary development phases identified stimuli that participants found unclear, too broad, or poorly matched to the intended item content; these stimuli were removed or replaced before the present data collection.

The final empirical task is under active proprietary development, so one administered image-pair item is reproduced in the main manuscript and the remaining pairs are described in a supplemental stimulus-audit table.
Unidimensional ordinal factor models for the graded-preference responses were fitted separately for STAI and SABAS in Mplus using ULSMV estimation and Theta parameterization.

Each observed pair response was treated as an ordinal manifestation of a latent utility difference, following Thurstonian logic for graded-preference data (Brown & Maydeu-Olivares, 2018; Maydeu-Olivares & Brown, 2010).

text.text: Because the empirical task had one ordinal response per pair rather than separate utility indicators for each image, the reduced model fixed the oriented pair loadings to the keyed pattern +1, -1, +1 for both instruments.

The model estimated four ordinal thresholds for each of the three five-category pair responses, yielding 12 threshold parameters and three degrees of freedom from the 12 thresholds plus three polychoric correlations.
Modelderived factor scores, model-implied information, average MAP-score standard errors, and empirical factor-score reliability were compared with the Likert benchmarks.

To test whether the empirical contrast depended on the constrained ordinal factor score, we also computed keyed GPC sum scores, first principal components, pair-level benchmark associations, and descriptive multitrait-multimethod correlations (Campbell & Fiske, 1959).

text.text: Supervised prediction models were used only as recovery benchmarks.

Ridge, LASSO, Elastic Net, and Random Forest models predicted the corresponding Likert total from the three GPC responses under nested cross-validation, with an outer 10-fold loop for performance estimation and an inner tuning loop.
Performance was summarized with out-of-sample Pearson correlations and RMSE relative to an intercept-only benchmark.
Benchmark recovery showed the central empirical contrast.
The STAI model-derived GPC factor score correlated .70 with the STAI-6 Likert total.
Keyed GPC sums and the first principal component recovered essentially the same benchmark signal, r = .71 and .71.

For SABAS, recovery was weak across the corresponding diagnostics: the model-derived GPC factor score correlated .18 with the SABAS Likert total, keyed sums correlated .17, and the first principal component correlated .16.

Figure 3 displays this descriptive multitrait-multimethod pattern, showing strong cross-method recovery for STAI and weak recovery for SABAS rather than a uniform advantage or failure of the GPC format.

text.text: The contrast was robust across flexible recovery benchmarks and pair-level checks.

Crossvalidated prediction from the three STAI GPC responses yielded r = .72 for ridge, r = .72 for LASSO, r = .72 for elastic net, and r = .70 for Random Forest, with RMSE values clearly below the intercept-only baseline of 4.25.
For SABAS, cross-validated r values ranged only from .18 to .26, and RMSE values were only slightly below the intercept-only baseline of 5.26.
Pair-level benchmark associations showed the same pattern: absolute pair-level correlations were .60, .68, and .56 for STAI, compared with .04, .07, and .21 for SABAS.
Reliability and ordinal model diagnostics helped interpret this contrast, but they did not replace benchmark recovery.
The Likert benchmarks showed acceptable internal consistency: alpha and omega were .84 and .84 for STAI-6, and .71 and .72 for SABAS.
The GPC response patterns diverged more sharply.
STAI-GPC showed ordinal alpha = .87 and ordinal omega = .88, whereas SABAS-GPC showed ordinal alpha = .31 and ordinal omega = .32.
Thus, the STAI image-pair responses formed a much more coherent keyed pattern than the SABAS image-pair responses.

text.text: Study 2 illustrates the design logic from Study 1 in a deliberately constrained empirical task.
The two implementations used the same nominal format, the same number of pairs, and the same broad analytic pipeline, but they preserved very different amounts of benchmark-relevant information.
The STAI implementation retained a strong recoverable signal across model-derived scoring, keyed and component scores, supervised prediction, and descriptive MTMM checks.
The SABAS implementation did not.
This contrast should not be read as proof that state anxiety is inherently compressible or that problematic smartphone application-based use is inherently non-compressible.

It shows that two same-format, same-length image-GPC implementations can generate radically different recovery profiles, without allowing the difference to be assigned causally to a single feature of the design.

The SABAS disadvantage may reflect weaker target signal, less coherent pair responses, construct underrepresentation, stronger non-target stimulus influence, or a mismatch between the current-moment image prompt and a benchmark concerning habitual smartphone application use.

This ambiguity illustrates the importance of distinguishing response format, construct representation, stimulus properties, pair construction, prompt framing, and scoring when evaluating ultra-short comparative assessments.

This article asked which design factors determine recovery in ultra-short GPC assessment, whether graded preferences retain more target information than binary paired choices, and whether empirical three-pair image-GPC implementations targeting different construct domains exhibit distinct benchmark-recovery profiles despite sharing the same response format and test length.
Three contributions follow from the two studies.
The first contribution is that recoverability is a property of the construct-stimulus-design system, not of test length or response format alone.
Study 1 showed that three GPC pairs can recover benchmark information when the target construct is focused, stimulus signal is strong, nuisance variance is low, and pair construction is balanced.
The same number of pairs failed when those conditions deteriorated.
Study 2 showed the same logic empirically: two implementations with the same three-pair image-GPC format produced very different levels of benchmark recovery.
This contribution also clarifies terminology.

Binary forced choice and graded paired comparison are not interchangeable, because dichotomizing comparative responses discards preferencestrength information that can contribute to recovery (Bech et al., 2007; Brown & Maydeu-Olivares, 2018; Stark et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Binary forced choice and graded paired comparison are not interchangeable, because dichotomizing comparative responses discards preferencestrength information that can contribute to recovery <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bech et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Brown & Maydeu-Olivares, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Stark et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: The second contribution is that reliability can be high for psychometrically undesirable reasons.
In Study 1, stronger systematic nuisance variance reduced benchmark recovery while increasing omega.

This pattern is important beyond the specific GPC design studied here: a response pattern can be internally coherent because respondents are reacting consistently to construct-irrelevant stimulus features.
Study 2 is consistent with the converse problem as well.
The STAI implementation showed both high keyed reliability and strong benchmark recovery, whereas the SABAS implementation showed weak keyed coherence and weak recovery.

Taken together, the two studies show why reliability must be interpreted alongside benchmark recovery, stimulus review, pair-level diagnostics, and local fit rather than treated as sufficient evidence that compression has succeeded.
The third contribution is that scoring methods cannot create construct information that is not represented in the responses.
In Study 1, cross-validated ridge prediction tracked the same design constraints as simpler recovery indices.
In Study 2, regularized linear models and Random Forests recovered the STAI benchmark well but did not rescue the SABAS implementation.
Supervised prediction is useful here because it estimates recoverable benchmark information out of sample.

It does not establish that the response process is valid, that stimuli represent the intended construct, or that scores are suitable for applied decisions (American Educational Research Association et al., 2014; Messick, 1995; Morris et al., 2019).
text.formatted: It does not establish that the response process is valid, that stimuli represent the intended construct, or that scores are suitable for applied decisions <ref type="bibr">(American Educational Research Association et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Messick, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Morris et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The findings translate into practical design guidance.

Before committing to a three-pair GPC form, developers should verify that the benchmark is sufficiently focused, candidate stimuli align semantically with the intended item content, pairs are balanced in target direction, and the prompt matches the time frame of the benchmark.

A three-pair design is most defensible when pair-level benchmark associations are consistently positive, keyed-pair reliability is not driven by an obvious non-target contrast, local residual diagnostics do not point to a single problematic pair, and cross-validated recovery improves meaningfully over an intercept-only baseline.
High alpha, omega, model-implied information, or small factor-score standard errors are insufficient on their own.

Increasing test length is most justified when the construct is heterogeneous, stimulus meanings cover only part of the benchmark domain, pair-level associations are uneven, nuisance features are salient, or recovery remains below the intended practical criterion despite acceptable internal consistency.
Several limitations should guide interpretation.
Study 1 used a simplified one-target, onenuisance data-generating model.
Real comparative assessments may involve multidimensional target constructs, multiple nuisance sources, local dependence, heterogeneous response thresholds, and person-by-stimulus interactions.
The focal and threshold-sensitivity simulations reduce some concerns, but they do not exhaust plausible design failures.
Study 2 was not a factorial experiment and should not be used to assign a single causal explanation to the SABAS result.
Its role is empirical delimitation: it asks whether two very short image-GPC implementations recover their verbal benchmarks strongly enough to be psychometrically informative.
The empirical image stimuli were developed through expert consensus and qualitative feedback, but they were not independently validated before deployment.
The sample was not demographically broad, and benchmark recovery may differ across age, cultural, linguistic, and educational groups.
Future work should manipulate response format, stimulus modality, test length, and pair construction within the same empirical design.

A stronger design would compare single-stimulus ratings, GPC preferences, and binary paired choices using the same stimulus pool, vary the number of pairs, and include independent ratings of stimulus construct relevance and nuisance features.
Adaptive or modular comparative designs may be especially useful because not all constructs or stimulus sets should be forced into the same number of comparisons (Wang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Adaptive or modular comparative designs may be especially useful because not all constructs or stimulus sets should be forced into the same number of comparisons <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Wang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In sum, ultra-short comparative assessment should begin with a design question: does the response pattern contain enough target-relevant information to make validity plausible?
When the answer is yes, a short GPC form may recover a benchmark efficiently.

When the answer is no, neither internal consistency, model-implied precision, nor flexible prediction can compensate for missing target information.     real item is shown to illustrate the administered prompt, image-pair layout, and five-category graded preference response scale; the remaining proprietary items are not reproduced. descriptive prediction scores, and model-derived GPC factor scores.
